note: Guided runs. add_guides.py copies each guide into the content file of its build. A guide plays a shipped operation at a fixed tier, seed and clock, so the operation itself does not change.

guides.title: Holdings in six turns
guides.blurb: A short run of The Manchurian Trap at Tier 1. Learn what a holding costs and when to give one up.

steps.text: This guided run lasts six turns at Tier 1. You hold the north and the south for the Nationalist government in 1946. Read the Holdings panel above the cards.
Each holding costs you every turn and denies the rival some leverage. Manchuria costs 2 and denies only 1, so the panel marks it consuming.
Give up Manchuria with the button in its row. The move costs 1 action and 2 legitimacy. You cannot take it back.
Manchuria no longer drains your armies. The south costs 1 and denies 2, so it still pays to keep.
You gave up the south, which cost 1 and denied the rival 2. Manchuria still costs more than it denies.
Open the operation log below the board. Each holding takes its cost from your shields first and then adds pressure.
The report at the end lists acts against your own position. Each turn you keep a consuming holding counts as one.

guides.title: Reach in six turns
guides.blurb: A short run of The Reach at Tier 1. Learn the three permits and what the rival may do that you may not.

steps.text: This guided run lasts six turns at Tier 1. You play the United States and its allies against the Party-state. Read the Reach panel above the cards.
Each act in Reach carries a permit for your side. Open acts cost nothing extra. Priced acts work and cost you. Closed acts stay barred to you.
Use an open act now. Designate the agencies and list the front organizations costs 1 action and shields your Legal domain.
Tap Why under a closed act. One card shows what lets the rival do it. Another shows what bars your side.

Screen people by ancestry and family ties has a price. The act works but costs 8 legitimacy and counts as an act against your own position. Ancestry is not loyalty, and the game charges you for treating it as one.
The rival just asked a firm abroad for its customer records under the 2017 law. Your panel lists that power as closed to you.
The report at the end lists what your rules closed. It counts how often the rival used each closed act.
